Introduction - September 2011
Introduction
• Increasing concerns about the state of the 
global economy and rising levels of risk aversion 
are now leading us to expect higher gold prices, 
and for longer, than we had hitherto been 
looking for.  We believe gold could pierce $2,000 
by year-end, and hold at elevated levels for 
at least the first half of 2012 as inflation fears 
tighten their grip on investor perceptions. 
• Gold’s rally through $1,900 intra-day in late 
August was accompanied by some investment 
buying at a “grass roots” level as investors 
feared that the market was running away from 
them.  The subsequent correction deterred 
buyers, but bullish sentiment prevails and we 
believe it is only a matter of time before fresh 
buying develops. 
• Silver continued, in the main, to underperform 
gold as investors remained bruised by the 
viciousness of the price fall in May.  The market 
still has to contend with a surplus of supply over 
fabrication demand, but the metal has been 
showing some signs of fresh investor interest 
and if gold runs towards $2,000 then silver 
could well test $50. 
• Platinum has outperformed palladium in 
recent weeks and, while this is partly because 
of palladium’s prior outperformance, platinum 
has also been supported by fears of supply 
disruption from South Africa.  There were clear 
signs of fresh interest when platinum slipped to 
a discount to gold in August. 
• With the gold market needing a period of price 
consolidation in order to underpin fresh demand, 
we should see platinum re-establish a premium 
over gold, but this could quickly evaporate if 
or when the yellow metal makes its dash for 
$2,000, unless fresh South African platinum 
supply scares emerge. 
• Platinum’s premium over palladium exceeded 
$1,100 at times during August.  The regional 
variations in the global economic outlook 
(favouring China and possibly North America 
over Europe, for example) suggest that this 
premium could narrow towards $1,000 in 
coming weeks.
Investor concerns remain focused on political leadership and 
governments’ ability to tackle persistent economic problems.  
Attention now turns in particular to the September meeting 
of the FOMC.

Precious Metals Supply-Demand Overview
There were a number of disappointing economic numbers 
released during August and both business and consumer 
confidence levels fell.  The associated reduction in consumer 
spending has, arguably, further weakened the putative 
economic recovery in North America and Europe, and equity    
markets suffered accordingly during much of August.  Dr. 
Bernanke’s statement at the Jackson Hole policy-makers’ 
conference late in the month met a mixed reception.  The 
equity markets picked up on the expectation that the 
September meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee 
(FOMC) would herald a further programme of economic 
support, although the nature of that likely support is still a 
subject of speculation.  Treasury markets also picked up, 
though, in the belief that any recovery will be anaemic.  
There are still some fears that the US economy is headed for 
a double-dip recession.
The minutes of the August meeting of the FOMC revealed 
divided opinions among Committee members about how 
best to address the faltering in the US economy.  In the 
event, the minutes implied a kind of “holding pattern”, with 
a vote to keep short-term interest rates at just above zero 
until at least the middle of 2013.  The Committee members 
noted that, while the effects of temporary factors such as 
the Japanese earthquake and the “damping effect” of higher 
energy and other commodity prices appeared to be waning, 
the “underlying strength of the economic recovery remained 
uncertain”.  Some members pointed also to “the financial 
market strains seen during the inter-meeting period, as 
contributing to a downgrade of the outlook for the economy”. 
These above factors were, almost by definition, supportive 
for gold.

Gold will also take support from the extension of the Fed’s 
loose monetary policy, especially as, in light of inflationary 
expectations, it points to negative real interest rates for an 
extended period.
The markets will now wait for a strong policy assertion from 
the FOMC meeting in September, especially as this meeting 
has been extended to two days from the original one-day 
schedule.  In late August, market sentiment is leaning 
towards expecting further asset purchases, although an 
extension of the maturity of Federal Reserve debt is also a 
viable possibility.
We should also point out, though, that even if the September 
meeting produces a statement that calms the markets’ 
nerves, we then have to head into another round of US  
debt negotiations in November with respect to public 
spending cuts and this is likely to raise more uncertainty in 
investors’ minds.
While the September meeting of the FOMC is therefore 
clearly very important, it will not be sufficient to quell 
market fears over either the outlook for economic activity, or 
inflationary concerns and gold will continue to benefit from 
investment at both the professional and the private level.

Gold’s spike and subsequent heavy recoil have not severed the 
price’s uptrends, either in the medium term, or in the shorter-
term.  Over the course of August, gold gained 12% in dollar terms.  
Silver, still struggling after the May fall and struggling with a poor 
economic outlook, gained just 5%, while platinum added 3%.  
Palladium lost 7% amid liquidation. 
Over the twelve months to end-August, silver gained 112%, while 
palladium rose by a net 51%.  Gold added 45%, while platinum 
added 21%.
The S&P high since January 2010 was registered in late April, as 
was that of the FT Eurozone.  The Bombay and Shenzhen A indices, 
by contrast, started turning down in November 2010.  At end-
August 2011, the S&P was the marginal outperformer, with a gain 
from January 2010 of 7% despite economic concerns.  Europe had 
shed 21%.
Over the month of August the same indices have struggled.  The 
S&P shed almost 6% and the Bombay market 9%, while the FT 
Eurozone slid by 12%.  The Shenzhen was more robust, losing 
just 3%.

were particularly heavy, both in the final approach to the 
highs and then in the subsequent correction, which lopped 
more than $200 off the price in the three days 23rd-25th 
August; fresh buying started to develop on the 25th and 
prices closed well off their lows.
The 24th saw a range of over $100, which gained substantial 
press coverage as the largest one-day fall since the 22nd 
January 1980, when gold sank by more than $120 in one 
day after reaching the then all-time record of $850.  In 
percentage terms, however, the August 2011 fall was smaller 
than the January 1980 drop, at 6% of the previous day’s fix, 
compared with 13% in the earlier fall.  
On a year-on-year basis, the end-August fix represented a 
gain of $567.50 or 46% and as such, it could be argued that 
there is not much scope for further price gain.  However, we 
take the view that the economic and financial environment 
remains strongly supportive of higher gold prices, and that 
these higher prices are now likely to be sustained for longer 
than we had originally expected.  For example:
•	
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) remains 
divided over the best course of action for underpinning 
the United States economy and a third round of 
quantitative easing cannot be ruled out, especially as the 
Federal Reserve Chairman Bernanke has now announced 
that the September FOMC meeting will be extended 
to two days, rather than the originally scheduled one-
day programme.  The minutes from the August FOMC 
meeting were released at the end of the month and 
showed that, after consideration of a range of options, 
the Committee had decided upon sustaining loose 
monetary policy at least through to mid-2013.  This, 
allied to already bloated fiscal balance sheets, points to 
increasing inflationary pressures and by association a 
long period of negative real interest rates; both of these 
traditionally favour gold investment.
Gold
Gold now looks likely to trade above $2,000 for at 
least the first half of 2012
Gold’s move above $1,900 during August lacked a degree 
of substance in that the underlying physical market was 
already struggling and also that some professional investors 
were ready to sell into the price strength.  The run was swift 
and sharp, fuelled in part by technical trading (i.e. stop-
loss orders and momentum trades).   It was followed by 
an equally sharp fall, but underlying sentiment remained 
positive towards gold, with the result that gold’s net change 
over the course of August was a gain of $200 or 12%, with 
an opening fix of $1,613.50 and a closing fix of $1813.50.
The second half of July saw gold prices contained in a 
relatively narrow range, but with a mild upward bias, 
between $1,580 and $1,625 (on an intraday basis).  Early 
August saw a swift jump towards $1,680 following a number 
of weak economic indictors that fuelled expectations of 
a further round of quantitative easing.  The move gained 
traction in the second week of August as fears increased 
over the possibility of a downgrade of French sovereign debt, 
due to that country’s exposure to European debt in the more 
heavily stricken nations, and prices jumped towards $1,815.  
After a brief correction gold then took off, gaining more than 
$120 in three days and clearing $1,900 on 23rd August.  
This move was, as noted above, extended by technical 
trading, but with sentiment also powered by disappointment 
at the outcome of the Franco-German summit with respect 
to how to tackle the problems in Europe.  Trading volumes

Gold, Major International Currencies; Medium Term
•	
Allied to this, the problems facing the Eurozone are 
still showing no sign of imminent resolution and, 
if anything, the balance of probabilities points to a 
worsening of the Eurozone sovereign debt position.  The 
recent consolidation of some domestic Greek banks is 
a partial solution but larger issues continue to prevail; 
some European commercial banks were reported to be 
using the European Central Bank’s emergency lending 
programmes in late August.
•	
Major currencies remain volatile and some central banks’ 
continued interest in accumulating gold is still attracting 
market comment as an indicator of reduced confidence 
in fiat currencies; this of itself is arguably supportive of 
gold market sentiment.
•	
Domestic inflation in China remains higher than the 
government would wish despite continued monetary 
tightening policies, meaning that local private investors 
are continuing to invest in gold.  Meanwhile there is also 
the persistent possibility of a bubble in the domestic 
property market and this, too, is informing gold 
investment both domestically and abroad.
•	
The turmoil in Libya, coupled with the possibility of 
renewed oil supplies from that country, may take some 
of the intensity out of political tension as well as easing 
pressure on the oil market, but this is not expected to 
work strongly against gold investment activity.
Price outlook; a period of consolation or  a minor 
correction is now likely before renewed strength in the 
fourth quarter of 2011 and into the first half of 2012
After the recent period of price volatility, it is helpful to look 
at the constructions of the price charts in order to gain a 
sense of perspective.  Gold entered an accelerated uptrend 
in early July.  In mid-August the spike upwards and the 
subsequent correction saw that trend briefly severed both to 
the upside and the downside, but these breaches were very 
short-lived and the upward trend remained in place at the 
start of September.  Furthermore, the shallower, longer-lived, 
uptrend provided support to the price when it was correcting. 
In essence, this now means that gold could afford a period of 
sideways trading, with support at $1,750, without severing 
the sharp uptrend.  Possibly more significantly, it could even 
afford to drop towards $1,700 during September without 
violating the shallower upward channel.

Gold - September 2011
From a fundamental standpoint, with the physical market 
fractured (see below), there is a theoretical possibility that 
the price could flatten during September as the market 
re-groups and some fresh buying support develops in the 
jewellery markets.  The foundations are, however, already 
in place for a move towards $2,000 during the final quarter, 
probably towards the end of the year, as economic and 
financial concerns intensify; inflationary and currency 
concerns are now likely to be sustained for longer than 
we had previously expected.  Investor appetite for gold is 
not now likely to be sated until the second half of 2012, or 
possibly into the early part of 2013.  
Physical investors (both in the investment bar and high-
caratage jewellery market) have shown flexibility in the past 
in terms of their acceptance of rising gold prices.  Recently 
there has been an interesting mix of market sentiment, 
which arguably points to a fresh acceptance of a higher gold 
price range, although this is still at an early stage and partly 
drives our argument for a period of sideways trading or 
indeed a further downward price correction.
Gold and the Inverse of the G6-weighted Dollar
Physical demand; virtually nonexistent in some places, 
but picking up into price strength in others
Physical demand patterns have been particularly interesting 
of late and the imminence of the Festival season in India, 
and the build-up towards Christmas in the west make for 
a fascinating outlook for the next few weeks.  One of the 
most interesting developments is that in parts of South-
east Asia, and also in parts of India, investors have been 
buying into rising prices, presumably on the basis that they 
were concerned that they would not have the benefit of a 
downward price correction in order to go “bargain-hunting”; 
then when the price fall developed they stood back from the 
market again.
It is by no means unusual for would-be investors to stand 
aside from a volatile market, whether prices are rising or 
falling, but the fact that buying was strong when prices  
were rising does point to an underlying bullish expectation  
in a number of buying regions and indicates the likelihood  
of a fresh body of buying interest emerging once prices  
have stabilised.

Strength in India and parts of the Far East...
In India, which accounted for over 530 tonnes of jewellery 
and investment products in the first half of 2011, demand 
has been more robust, with buying in evidence both into the 
rising price and during the fall.  At the end of August the 
market remained reasonably strong, with the Ahmedabad 
market trading at a premium to the international market.  
The latest news on the monsoon shows that, over the 
country as a whole, rainfall since the start of June has been 
just 1% below the long-term average and this bodes well 
for the harvest and, by implication, gold purchases as the 
festival seasons develop.  Diwali, traditionally the most 
auspicious day in the year for gift-giving, falls on 26th 
October this year and it is possible that some of the recent 
buying in the market has been in advance of this Festival 
(the Festival as a whole lasts for five days, commencing with 
Dhanteras and culminating with Diwali itself).
... but there are also clear patches of weakness
Demand patterns in South-East Asia have been mixed.  
In Indonesia, for example, the recently-ended period of 
Ramadan, building up to the Eid festival, would normally be 
expected to be a strong period for gold jewellery demand 
but this year there has been very little interest and some 
jewellery stockists have been finding themselves forced to 
melt inventory in order to meet financial commitments.  On 
the other hand, demand for investment products has been 
strong, largely in the small bar market.  This was particularly 
the case when the price was surging higher; furthermore the 
innate bullishness in the market has meant that scrap flows 
have been limited.  Patterns have been similar in Thailand, 
although there has been more of a “trading” mentality, with 
Official Sector Gold Holdings
some profit taking developing in times of price strength 
and some private would-be investors have been slightly 
scared by the volatility in price.  Demand also remains under 
pressure in the Middle East and here, too, there are signs in 
places of liquidation of fabricator inventory.

Quarterly Silver Price & Forecast
Silver
Still underperforming gold and there is still a risk of 
some further downward correction towards $38-$39.
In our most recent One Year Forecast we recalled silver’s 
notorious reputation for volatility and warned of the 
possibility of a spike upwards or downwards during August.  
In the event, neither developed; rather, silver traded in a 
comparatively narrow range given that gold was soaring.  
In fact, gold and silver traded in almost exactly the same 
range, on a percentage basis, as each other.  Silver’s 
intraday August trade was between approximately $37.20 
and $44.20, a range of 18.8% with an intra-month change of 
5.2% to close August at  $41.35 (basis the fix).  Gold’s range 
of $1,608-$1,911 was also 18.8%, although gold’s intra-
month change was 12%.
Still leaning towards the base metals rather than gold
There are at least two likely reasons for silver’s relative 
underperformance by comparison with gold.  The first dates 
back to the calamitous price falls in the silver market in May, 
dragging the rest of the commodities complex down with 
it.  This reminded investors of how volatile the metal can 
be, and therefore frightened away some less experienced or 
more nervous would-be market participants.  Gold investors 
are more confident, and support in the gold market has been 
more solid than it has in silver.  Furthermore the markets 
remain aware of official sector diversification into gold, while 
central banks are still net sellers of silver.
In addition, while silver’s industrial demand may improve 
by perhaps 7% this year, total fabrication is still lower than 
the level of supply into the market and silver therefore has 
to contend with a surplus again this year, as it will in 2012.  
Nagging concerns about the economic outlook, therefore, 
have helped to undermine silver’s performance while giving 
gold an extra boost.  Dr. Bernanke’s Jackson Hole comments, 
in which he neither ruled in nor ruled out a further bout 
of quantitative easing (but certainly hinted strongly at the 
Fed’s determination to give the economy a fillip if possible) 
boosted gold but gave silver only a slight lift, even though 
the equity markets also rallied, as did the PGMs.
This would tend to confirm that the silver market is still 
nervous as we enter September and for the time being it still 
looks likely to underperform the rest of the sector.
Outlook; still in need of further consolidation, while 
we also expect that gold’s positive medium-term 
prospects will eventually take silver higher, peaking in 
the first half of 2012
Although gold has already tested, and essentially failed, 
at the $1,900 level, that late-August run was much more 
of a speculatively and technically-fuelled spike than a 
solid performance based on firm-handed investment (the 
liquidations in the gold ETFs during the spike are testament 
to this).  With the Eurozone still struggling with sovereign 
debt and the Chinese economy also showing more signs of 
slowing, quite apart from the economic conditions in the 
United States, silver investors were not prepared to chase 
gold higher during August.
The outlook for the world economy remains very cautious 
for the coming months and silver’s fundamental position 
suggests that it should continue to underperform gold.

Physical demand is likely to start to gather some pace,

then gold will benefit from long-term investment and silver is

perfectly possible that the gold:silver ratio, which stands

The demand outlook is improving gradually...
As we move into September the physical silver market 
should start to pick up, especially in India, where there is 
still some investor preference for silver because of gold’s 
very high price.  Local sentiment is becoming increasingly 
robust and some Indian traders are looking for local price 
gains of up to 10% in the coming weeks.  As we write, 
silver is trading in Ahmedabad at around Rps 62,000/kg and 
some traders are expecting to trade at Rps 70,000/kg as 
the festival season gets underway.  Diwali, or the Festival 
of Lights, is traditionally the most important festival for the 
giving of gifts; gold generally takes the spotlight, but silver 
is also traditional.  Diwali falls this year on 26th October, 
so buying pressure is not likely to develop too early in 
September but, if the local market sentiment is bullish, then 
some buying may well be brought forward.
The latest Indian government report for the development 
of this year’s monsoon season shows that the country 
as a whole has received just 1% less rain this year 
when compared with the long period average (although 
August rains have been very heavy).  This can probably 
be construed as a reasonably healthy result and should 
underpin demand for gold and silver in the festival seasons.

second quarter of 2011 had a stark effect on the local silver

Investor activity;  creeping buying developing, but

Professional investment demand for silver, as indicated by 
the major exchange traded instruments, is slowly recovering 
from the very heavy sales of May through to July.  During 
that period the major funds between them suffered net 
redemptions of just over 1,900 tonnes in almost 11 weeks;  
an annualised redemption rate of over 9,000 tonnes.  Trading 
since mid-July has been patchy, but some 400 tonnes have 
been taken in since then.  The market does still remain 
nervous and the funds are prone to bouts of liquidation, 
suggesting that there is still something of a small speculative 
element using the instruments.  At the end of August the 
major funds held 17,656 tonnes, a net drop of just over 
1,000 tonnes since the start of the year.
Sentiment on Comex was more positive during August  and 
trading volumes were extremely heavy, both on “up and 
“down” days, suggesting a nervous market that is trading 
with tight stops.  Among the non-commercial and non-
reportable positions, the net long continued to fall in the 
early part of August as prices fell from $42 towards $37. 
The price run from $37 towards $44 over the subsequent 
fortnight was accompanied by 1,300 tonnes of fresh longs 
and short covering of 529 tonnes, taking the net position to 
7,325 tonnes, the largest since mid-April, but just below the 
twelve-month average.  (ETF investors were sellers in the 
first week of that fortnight’s bull run, only turning around in

spiky action, but the market needs to demonstrate that the 
floor between $33 and $37 remains solid.  Then the way will 
open up for renewed strength in line with gold and a possible 
test of $50 in late 2011/early 2012.

Both metals have effectively been trading “sideways” since 
the start of 2011.  With the exception of a few, very short-
lived spikes down towards $1,650, platinum has generally 
found support in the region of $1,700, and resistance 
between $1,890 and $1,920.  Taken over the longer term, 
however, platinum has broken below its long-term uptrend 
and is now starting to find resistance from the upward-
trending channel that had previously been offering support.  
Palladium has regularly found support between $700 and 
$720, while $800-820 has generally defined the upper 
boundary of palladium’s range in 2011 to date.
Platinum remains in a surplus of supply over demand,  
while palladium is in a global deficit and it is therefore 
arguable that the platinum-palladium premium, which has 
recently been in excess of $1,100, is likely to narrow again 
over the coming months and, on an average basis, at least, 
to trade below $1,000 towards the end of this year.  Once 
the Eurozone economy shows signs of a sustainable  
recovery then the premium may well rise again because  
of the importance of the EU auto industry to platinum  
market sentiment.
Considering Palladium, one also has to take sales from 
Russian government stocks into account.  These were 
estimated at approximately 0.8M ounces in 2010 and we 
believe that they will be at a similar level this year, before 
starting to tail off in 2012 and again in 2013.  We continue  
to expect that sales from this source will start to dwindle  
in the near future and that they may well have dried up 
within the next three years.  This points to a robust medium-
term outlook, but in the recent past palladium investors 
appear to have been suffering from an degree of fatigue, 
stemming from persistent concerns over key elements of the 
global economy. 
Platinum and palladium
Slightly different paths in August, with platinum the   
outperformer as palladium corrected from its July run
Platinum and palladium diverged slightly during August; 
with platinum registering a small gain overall, but palladium 
dropping in price.  At the start of August platinum continued 
the sideways course that it had been trading in the latter 
part of July, while palladium came under pressure more or 
less from the outset.
Platinum then staged a sharp fall (and palladium’s decline 
also accelerated sharply) on the 4th and 5th of August, in 
response to weak economic data that also put the base 
metals under pressure.  Platinum bounced swiftly, however, 
attracting some investment activity, as it moved to a 
discount to gold early in August, and then again later in 
the month when Chinese economic numbers showed fresh 
signs of improvement.  Support also developed as a result 
of concern over the continuity of South African mine supply, 
with some mining companies still in wage negotiations,  
and there is still some fear of disruption to Eskom power 
output with workers threatening strike action at that 
organisation also.
Palladium’s recovery was more anaemic and while platinum 
continued to make gains in the second half of August, 
palladium traded sideways, building support between $735 
and $740, but also running into some powerful resistance 
between $765 and $770.

Although platinum remains in a surplus of supply over 
demand, there is still potential for fresh investment.  The 
precious sector as a whole is likely to benefit from persistent 
(and potentially intensifying) inflationary forces in late 
2011 and through 2012, especially with the United States 
committed to a loose monetary policy for another two years.  
Furthermore the prospect for sustained strong Chinese 
growth, coupled with domestic inflationary forces, will 
underpin precious metals demand overall and, because of 
the importance of Chinese jewellery to platinum demand this 
is likely also to have a positive effect on market sentiment.
There is also, of course the risk of a drop in price in 
coming weeks if and when the South African mining 
sector establishes wage agreements.  For the longer term, 
though, the Managing Director of Eskom continues to stress 
the power utility will need to husband its resources and 
infrastructure carefully through 2012, as new power capacity 
is not due to begin coming on-stream until 2013 and there

affected next year. 
We can foresee platinum struggling in the near term as the 
Eurozone problems remain a source of concern, and ahead 
of renewed US debt negotiations in November, both of 
which are likely to unsettle sentiment with respect to global 
growth.  Once these US negotiations are out of the way, 
the path should be clearer, allowing for an improvement in

In the short term the price is likely to drift, as the

struggle to make headway above $1,870 in the next few

declined.  The net long position then increased by 1.7M

1.7M ounces, a 28-week high, with the increase driven 
not only by fresh buying, but substantial short covering.  
The early-August sell-off was in very heavy volume; the 
turnaround saw less dramatic turnover, but the market was 
still very busy.
Palladium activity was also more cautious on Nymex.  
Liquidation in mid-August was not reversed in the latter part 
of the month, and although some short covering did develop, 
the market was still experiencing long liquidation.  The latest 
August figures reflected a net investor position on Nymex of 
1.4M ounces, and a gross long position of 1.7M ounces.
As of 23rd August, the net palladium long position was 
considerably lower than the twelve-month average, while 
that of platinum was substantially higher, pointing towards a 
potential rebalancing and a narrowing of the premium that 
platinum has been commanding over palladium.
